KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 2:50 PM EDT...An area of showers that are
remnants of an early morning MCS that moved across western NY 
are currently tracking across our region south of I-90. These 
showers have sustained themselves a little longer than 
previously thought likely due to multiple MCVs that helped to 
locally increase lift. However, current mesoanalysis shows a 
very tight instability gradient near our western border with 
BGM, so they should continue to weaken the further east they 
track. So, no severe weather or flooding expected through the 
few hours. Most of our region is actually in a cold air damming 
setup thanks to sfc high pressure located over southeastern 
Canada. We lowered temps and dew points several degrees from the
NBM, with afternoon highs expected to be mainly in the 60s 
(terrain) to low 70s (valleys). 

For this evening and tonight: GOES 16 WV imagery shows a strong 
cosed upper low near James Bay, with a closer upper ridge centered 
over Tennessee. Between these features, an upper impulse embedded in 
the fast flow aloft will track over the Great Lakes and Northeast 
this evening into tonight. Current radar already shows storms firing 
over southern Ontario with this feature, and these are expected to 
grow upscale into an MCS this afternoon/evening before tracking into 
our area. 

A N/S oriented warm front is currently located over central NY, 
separating a very moist and unstable airmass from a much cooler and 
more stable airmass. How far east this front is able to make it this 
evening will determine how far east the threat for severe weather 
will extend. Outflow from the AM convection seems to have reinforced 
the cool side of the boundary/pushed it back west down towards the 
Catskills and Southern Tier. However, current satellite imagery 
shows quite a bit of clearing and instability beginning to 
build west of our Mohawk Valley and very close to our ADKs. If 
the warm front and instability are able to push closer/into the 
ADKs and western Mohawk Valley, this would increase the severe 
threat for these areas this evening. Further east, guidance is 
in good agreement for steepening mid-level lapse rates 
associated with a weak EML plume to allow for some elevated 
instability to work its way into our area, although SBCAPE looks
to be very limited. Given expected sharp instability gradient, 
there remains some uncertainty in just how far east the severe 
threat will extend. SPC has left their D1 convective outlook 
across our region unchanged, with the marginal risk mainly just 
for our western areas. However, given current satellite and 
mesoanalysis trends, we can't rule out a few stronger storms as 
far east as the Hudson Valley or even Taconics this 
evening/tonight. Main threats would be damaging winds with the 
MCS that is expected to develop, but large hail also very much 
remains on the table given the presence of elevated instability,
very favorable shear profiles (long straight hodographs), and 
elevated convection tracking on the cool side of the sfc 
boundary. Closer to the boundary itself in western Herkimer 
County, there looks to be more helicity (>200 m2s2 0-1 km 
layer), so an isolated tornado can't totally be ruled out 
although the probability is relatively low.

Other threat this evening/tonight with the MCS will be for heavy 
rain leading to flash flooding. There was some consideration to 
issuing a flood watch for the western Mohawk Valley and eastern 
Catskills along our border with BGM, but opted not to as the heavier 
rain this morning leading to more primed soils remained mainly west 
us. Our CWA only saw 0.1 to 0.25 inches per the NYS mesonet, and the 
areas that did see rain (mainly Catskills) also missed some of the 
heavier rain over the last couple days. Nevertheless, the 
environment looks favorable for heavy rain this evening and tonight 
with PWATs expected to 1.7 - 1.9" and warm cloud depths >12 kft. 
Rainfall rates of 1-2" per hour will be possible with the MCS. Main 
concerns would be on the southern side where more backbuilding and 
training is possible. Where training occurs, isolated 2-3" rainfall 
amounts can't be ruled out. WPC has maintained their marginal to 
slight risk ERO for our region, so will mention isolated to maybe 
scattered instances of flash flooding are possible, but just not 
widespread enough to justify a flood watch at this time. 

Timing of this MCS has sped up slightly compared to yesterday's 
forecast, so it should largely be out of our area by or around 12z 
Thursday. The warm front may lift back north into the Mid Hudson 
Valley tomorrow, with up to 1000-2000 J/kg of SBCAPE expected to 
build south of I-90. Deep layer shear remains impressive at 35-45 
kt, so on paper the environment appears favorable for a few strong 
storms. However, there remains a signal for fairly strong mid-level
